course_description:
The course introduces participants to the many challenges that affect agriculture and food systems across global regions. The course is relevant to students of agriculture and food science, agribusiness, and rural development. It equips participants to apply and extend knowledge and acquire skills for a rapidly changing world. Analysis of global megatrends, futuring and foresighting skills, globalisation, food security, climate change and followed by seeking solutions for sustainability and resilience. Participants are guided in their development as leaders who shape the future, emphasising self-directed learning that is guided by international experts.

This course uses a combination of lectures and tutorials, individual and group work, to develop your awareness of these global challenges, and help you consider how they affect your future professional practice. The course is designed to build upon the Leadership course (AGRC7046) most students will have completed in Semester 1, but if you have not yet taken that course (or it is not compulsory for you), you will not be disadvantaged. This course is offered on both St Lucia and Gatton campuses, and externally. The lectures will be posted on-line each week.

At the School of Agriculture and Food Sustainability, we are committed to creating an inclusive and empowering learning environment for all students. We value and respect the diverse range of experiences our students bring to their education, and we believe that this diversity is crucial for fostering a rich culture of knowledge-sharing and meaningful exploration. We hold students and staff accountable for actively contributing to establishing a respectful and supportive learning environment.

Bullying, harassment, and discrimination in any form are strictly against our principles and against UQ Policy, and will not be tolerated. If you have any concerns about your experience in this course, we encourage you to tell a member of the course teaching team. Your well-being and a positive learning atmosphere are of utmost importance to us.

course_aims: This course aims to develop students' understandings of a set of global challenges affecting agriculture, food and the environment. Furthermore, together with the companion course AGRC7046, we aim to develop personal leadership skills and motivate students to contribute to solving these challenges in their professional and personal capacities.

learning_outcomes.description: Analyse global challenges in agriculture, food, and rural development to identify their causes, interconnections, and implications.
Evaluate the role of your discipline in responding to complex global agricultural problems.
Communicate evidence-based insights clearly and persuasively to diverse audiences.
Justify ethical and socially responsible approaches to agricultural transformation.
Collaborate in interdisciplinary teams to explore sustainable agricultural responses.
Articulate your leadership potential to influence sustainable futures in agriculture and food systems.

assessment_details.title: Critical analysis report (group)
assessment_details.task_description: For this assessment, you will be working in groups of three or four. You will randomly be assigned to a group by the course coordinator in Week 1. As a group, select one of a set of articles to be provided on Blackboard. These address an issue related to global food security, agroecosystem sustainability, and/or sustainable resource use. Prepare a critical analysis of the selected manuscript (3,500 words, excluding references) based on course lecture content and an independent review of relevant literature. In your critical analysis, you should: Evaluate the article. Your assessment must be more than simply a summary. You should identify and explain the argument presented by the author(s). Form your own objective opinion. Based on course lecture content and your own independent reading (review of relevant literature): What assumptions underpin the authors' argument? Which perspectives or stakeholders are represented or overlooked? What evidence is convincing, uncertain, or contested? How well do the proposed solutions address the complexity of the challenge? What alternative argument would you put forth related to the subject of the selected article? Support your opinion. Use references from relevant scientific literature to support your stated opinion. Proposed structure: Introduction (200–300 words) Summary of the article's central argument (400–500 words) Critical evaluation of the argument (1,200 words) Integration with broader literature (900 words) Alternative perspective or recommendations (500–600 words) Conclusion (200 words) All students in the group MUST submit a copy of the report - all group members must be clearly identified on the assessment coversheet. How to write a critical analysis Some information about how to write a critical analysis / critical review paper is available at: http://depts.washington.edu/pswrite/Handouts/CriticalAnalysisPapers.pdf https://student.unsw.edu.au/writing-critical-review A review of relevant refereed literature A review of relevant refereed literature is part of this assignment. Do not rely on web pages alone as this will limit the rigour of your review. References (in order of importance) might include: Review papers in peer reviewed journals – very useful; recent reviews will have numerous references you can follow up. Original articles in peer reviewed journals. Academic books – also will have references you can follow up. Popular science articles (e.g. Australian Cotton or Grain growers magazines; online science news The Conversation ). Government agency and university websites. Government (.gov.au), CSIRO (csiro.au), University (.edu in the US or .edu.au) etc. are credible web resources. Popular websites. In general, avoid popular websites because they do not contain original information and what is presented has generally been re-interpreted. Some of the better sites tell you where the information comes from and you can use the popular site to find original source material. Please use APA 7th referencing style https://guides.library.uq.edu.au/referencing/apa7 Any criterion not addressed in the assignment will earn 0% (0 marks). See the attached critical analysis assessment matrix for additional detail. assessment_details.title: Critical analysis reflection (individual)
assessment_details.task_description: In addition to the group report, each student must submit an individual reflection (approximately 500 words). The reflection provides an opportunity to critically consider your own learning throughout the process of completing the assessment. Rather than summarising the group report, you should reflect on how engaging with the selected article, the broader literature, and discussions within your group influenced your understanding of the global challenge. Your reflection should address the following questions: How did your understanding of the issue evolve during the assessment? Which course concepts or theories most influenced your thinking? Were there perspectives, assumptions or trade-offs that you had not previously considered? How did discussions within your group challenge or reinforce your own views? What insights from this assessment will influence how you approach complex global challenges in the future? The reflection should demonstrate thoughtful engagement with your learning rather than simply describing the group's activities. assessment_details.title: Policy critique project
assessment_details.task_description: Select one of the government policy documents listed on Blackboard that addresses a major global challenge related to agriculture, food systems, water, climate change, biodiversity, sustainability, or the food–water–energy nexus. You will prepare a written policy critique that critically evaluates the selected policy using concepts, theories, and evidence introduced throughout the course. Policies are statements of principles or courses of action adopted (or proposed) by governments or organisations. They guide decision-making and shape responses to complex societal issues. In this course, you will focus on public policy related to global agricultural and environmental challenges. Policies may also be referred to as strategies, plans, frameworks, or schemes. A defining characteristic of policy is that it “provides the rules of engagement as well as steering a course for future generations” (Haigh 2012). Public policies are intended to improve societal outcomes and are often shaped by scientific evidence, political priorities, stakeholder interests, ethical considerations, and institutional constraints. You will prepare a policy critique of approximately 3,000 words (excluding references). Your critique should draw on: course lecture material, independent academic literature, systems thinking, and critical analysis. Your critique should address the following components: Policy Context and Purpose: Outline the policy issue and the intended outcomes of the selected policy. Provide relevant background and context, which may include: historical development, political or institutional context, key stakeholders, implementation challenges, and any significant revisions or controversies. What does the responsible government body hope to achieve through this policy? 2. Scientific and Evidence Base: Critically assess the scientific basis of the selected policy using peer-reviewed literature and other credible evidence sources. Consider: Does the policy demonstrate strong links between science and decision-making? Is the policy aligned with the best available scientific knowledge? Where is the policy scientifically defensible? Where could it be strengthened through greater integration of scientific evidence? 3. Alignment with Sustainability and the SDGs: Evaluate how well the selected policy aligns with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). You may consider: synergies between goals, trade-offs, unintended consequences, and tensions between environmental, social, and economic priorities. 4. Long-Term Sustainability Implications: Evaluate the potential long-term sustainability implications of implementing the selected policy. Your discussion may include: implications for food security, impacts on energy use or water allocation, environmental sustainability, equity and social justice considerations, resilience, and the influence of globalisation or international markets. You should critically examine how the policy may affect interconnected agricultural, environmental, and social systems over time. 5. Policy recommendations and pathways to change Based on your analysis, critically evaluate how the selected policy could be strengthened. Your discussion should consider: proposed policy improvements; opportunities to strengthen sustainability outcomes; governance and institutional arrangements; leadership and collaboration required for implementation; barriers, trade-offs and unintended consequences; the role of evidence, communication and interdisciplinary practice in supporting policy change. Drawing on course concepts, justify your recommendations and explain how they could contribute to more sustainable agricultural and food systems. Referencing Please use APA 7th referencing style (see UQ Library guidelines). References DAFF 2013, National Food Plan: Our Food Future , Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry, Canberra. Haigh, Y. 2012, Public Policy in Australia: Theory and Practice , Oxford University Press, Melbourne. Any criterion not addressed in the assignment will earn 0% (0 marks). Late submission of assessment will only be granted for documented medical reasons, accident, bereavement, jury service and other circumstances allowed in the UQ Policies and Procedures Library (PPL).

assessment_details.ai_statement:
Select one of the government policy documents listed on Blackboard that addresses a major global challenge related to agriculture, food systems, water, climate change, biodiversity, sustainability, or the food–water–energy nexus. You will prepare a written policy critique that critically evaluates the selected policy using concepts, theories, and evidence introduced throughout the course. Policies are statements of principles or courses of action adopted (or proposed) by governments or organisations. They guide decision-making and shape responses to complex societal issues. In this course, you will focus on public policy related to global agricultural and environmental challenges. Policies may also be referred to as strategies, plans, frameworks, or schemes. A defining characteristic of policy is that it “provides the rules of engagement as well as steering a course for future generations” (Haigh 2012). Public policies are intended to improve societal outcomes and are often shaped by scientific evidence, political priorities, stakeholder interests, ethical considerations, and institutional constraints. You will prepare a policy critique of approximately 3,000 words (excluding references). Your critique should draw on: course lecture material, independent academic literature, systems thinking, and critical analysis. Your critique should address the following components: Policy Context and Purpose: Outline the policy issue and the intended outcomes of the selected policy. Provide relevant background and context, which may include: historical development, political or institutional context, key stakeholders, implementation challenges, and any significant revisions or controversies. What does the responsible government body hope to achieve through this policy? 2. Scientific and Evidence Base: Critically assess the scientific basis of the selected policy using peer-reviewed literature and other credible evidence sources. Consider: Does the policy demonstrate strong links between science and decision-making? Is the policy aligned with the best available scientific knowledge? Where is the policy scientifically defensible? Where could it be strengthened through greater integration of scientific evidence? 3. Alignment with Sustainability and the SDGs: Evaluate how well the selected policy aligns with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). You may consider: synergies between goals, trade-offs, unintended consequences, and tensions between environmental, social, and economic priorities. 4. Long-Term Sustainability Implications: Evaluate the potential long-term sustainability implications of implementing the selected policy. Your discussion may include: implications for food security, impacts on energy use or water allocation, environmental sustainability, equity and social justice considerations, resilience, and the influence of globalisation or international markets. You should critically examine how the policy may affect interconnected agricultural, environmental, and social systems over time. 5. Policy recommendations and pathways to change Based on your analysis, critically evaluate how the selected policy could be strengthened. Your discussion should consider: proposed policy improvements; opportunities to strengthen sustainability outcomes; governance and institutional arrangements; leadership and collaboration required for implementation; barriers, trade-offs and unintended consequences; the role of evidence, communication and interdisciplinary practice in supporting policy change. Drawing on course concepts, justify your recommendations and explain how they could contribute to more sustainable agricultural and food systems. Referencing Please use APA 7th referencing style (see UQ Library guidelines). References DAFF 2013, National Food Plan: Our Food Future , Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry, Canberra. Haigh, Y. 2012, Public Policy in Australia: Theory and Practice , Oxford University Press, Melbourne. Any criterion not addressed in the assignment will earn 0% (0 marks).
